name: Umar Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and we don't take sides. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick and pack at a building supplies warehouse, the big one that serves the trade counters across the region. It's heavy stuff: bags of plaster, boxes of tiles, radiators, lengths of pipe. I'm in at six, I grab my scanner gun and a cage trolley, and I build orders until two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and honest, and the crew is good, we pray, eat and joke together. The pay is decent because of the heavy-goods allowance. What wears me out is the scanner gun telling me I'm two per cent behind rate when I've just lifted forty bags of cement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds right to me. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't see what it would do with a bag of plaster. So I'd expect my job to stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says. There's always a new gadget, and somebody still has to carry the bag of plaster. I've never used an AI thing in my life. I don't go online much, so it would be the lads at break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I'm getting married to Samira next summer, and I've got the wedding money and nearly a year of savings put away. I want things steady, and this is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do exactly what I'm doing. Six till two, save for the house, pay for the wedding without a loan. Maybe overtime on Saturdays before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides how things go in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira and I decide together, but I'll be the main earner once we have children, and that's how we both want it. So I need the steady wage. Her family would want to see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, a little. My uncle did this work for 25 years and he can't tie his shoes now. But I'm 27, so I've got a good while before I worry about that.

say: There's always a **new gadget**, but somebody still has to carry the load.
I'd say it to the **lads at break**, not online.
think: I'm **glad**, because I want things steady before the wedding.
I've got the **wedding money** and nearly a year of savings put away.
do: Keep working **six till two** on the heavy-goods picking line.
Take **Saturday overtime** before the wedding to pay without a loan.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like a normal Monday.
S0.quote: There's always a new gadget, and somebody still has to carry the bag of plaster. I've never used an AI thing in my life.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **heavy goods** feeling hard to automate.
The **wedding** next summer frames everything he decides.
He sees himself as the future **main earner**, by choice with his fiancée.

steps.text: Keep working the six-till-two heavy-goods picking shift
Take Saturday overtime to pay for the wedding without a loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office people get hit first. The ones who book the lorries and answer the trade customers. The robots come into our side more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say leave the floor alone, it works. Every time the office changes a system, we're the ones who lose an afternoon fixing it. I'd tell the manager that to his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think it won't reach me for a long time. A robot that picks a bent length of copper pipe off a rack is a long way off. The pick rate targets are what would get worse. That happens once the office gets clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I wouldn't go on any AI courses, that's not me. I'd keep saving and maybe put the house search back by six months to be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not about my job tomorrow, more about the company squeezing us harder with smarter targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on courses. What if the company offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it part of the job, I'd go and sit there. But I wouldn't choose it. I'd rather learn from my uncle, who fits bathrooms, than from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the squeeze came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers who sit upstairs and never lift anything. And honestly the government, for taxing small firms until only the giant ones survive. The giant ones love machines.

say: Leave the **floor alone**, because it already works fine.
Every office system change costs us **an afternoon** fixing it.
think: A robot picking **bent copper pipe** is a long way off.
Smarter office software would push our **pick rate targets** up.
do: Keep **heads down** and turn down optional AI courses.
Push the **house search** back by six months to be careful.
Keep **saving** the heavy-goods allowance each month.
feel: **Uneasy** about harder targets, not about losing the job tomorrow.
S1.quote: A robot that picks a bent length of copper pipe off a rack is a long way off. The pick rate targets are what would get worse.
fieldNote: He fears **tougher targets** more than robots in this picture.
He blames **managers upstairs** and taxes that favour big firms.
He'd rather learn from his **uncle** than from a screen.

steps.text: Keep working the heavy-goods line and skip optional AI courses
Bank the heavy-goods allowance into savings every month
Put the house search with Samira back six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one is frightening. Two years for the thinking machines, then 2031 for robots that can lift like me. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the government should slow it down, put rules on these companies. I don't like government meddling, but this is too fast for any family. I'd sign a petition, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd lose this job and I don't know what I'd do. The office side goes in 2028, that's the rotas and the orders, but the lifting is still me for three years. I don't see why a company would keep a man who needs breaks and prayer time once the robots can lift like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop the house search and keep the savings as cash. I'd still marry Samira, nobody's stopping that, but we'd have a small wedding and save the difference. Then I'd ask my uncle about learning bathroom fitting, because people will want a person in their home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night, doing sums in my head. It would feel like the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having three years before the robots change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is enough to learn a trade from my uncle, if I start the first week. But I'm slow with new things, I know that about myself. I'd need someone to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have the wedding. Would anything else about your family plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Children, maybe. We'd want them soon, but I wouldn't want a baby arriving the same year my job goes. I'd talk to Samira's father, and to the imam, and ask what they'd do.

say: The government should **slow it down** with rules, even though I hate meddling.
I'd **sign a petition** for the first time in my life.
think: I'd **lose this job** by 2031 and don't know what comes next.
The **lifting** stays mine for three years after the office side goes.
do: Stop the **house search** and keep all savings in cash.
Hold a **small wedding** and save the difference.
Ask his uncle to teach him **bathroom fitting** in the first week.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake at night doing sums, like the ground is moving.
S2.quote: I don't see why a company would keep a man who needs breaks and prayer time once the robots can lift like me.
fieldNote: Strong savings don't calm him: he expects to **lose the job** outright.
His free-market views **bend** under this speed; he'd back rules.
He'd turn to **family and faith** before any government scheme.

steps.text: Stop the house search and hold savings in cash
Scale the wedding with Samira down to a small one
Learn bathroom fitting from his uncle starting the first week
Ask Samira's father and the imam for advice on children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. Better than two, but still too fast for a man like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that the big firms are moving too fast. But I'd also say people should look after their own, family first. I don't want a government cheque, I want work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait. Five years sounds long, and I'd tell myself I'll start learning next year, then the year after. I know that about myself, and it's not good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and the heavy-goods allowance as long as I could. I'd still buy a small house with Samira, nearer my uncle, so I can help him on Saturdays. That's half a trade without calling it a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the fast one, but I'd feel it every time the manager walks the floor with a stranger in a suit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it with my own eyes. If a robot came to our site and picked a cement bag, I'd be at my uncle's the next morning. Until then, I'd believe it when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much needs cutting, we live simply. Maybe the new car I wanted. My old one runs fine.

say: The big firms are **moving too fast** for ordinary workers.
People should look after their own, **family first**, and want work, not cheques.
think: I'd probably **put off** learning anything new, year after year.
I know that **delay** is a weakness of mine.
do: Keep the job and **heavy-goods allowance** as long as possible.
Buy a **small house** near his uncle with Samira.
Help his uncle with **bathrooms on Saturdays** as a half-trade.
feel: **Anxious**, especially when the manager walks a stranger in a suit around.
S3.quote: If a robot came to our site and picked a cement bag, I'd be at my uncle's the next morning. Until then, I'd believe it when I see it.
fieldNote: He is **candid** that he'd waste warning time by waiting.
His plan is a **half-trade** through Saturday work with his uncle.
He'd skip the **new car** but sees little else to cut.

steps.text: Keep the warehouse job until a robot reaches the site
Buy a small house near his uncle with Samira
Help his uncle fit bathrooms on Saturdays
Drop plans for a new car and keep the old one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be 39 or 40, with children at school. That's a whole different life by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is fair warning, and nobody can blame anyone if they don't get ready. Fathers should be learning a trade for their kids' sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the warehouse job in the end, I'm sure of that. But ten years of Saturdays with my uncle is a real trade. By 2039 I'd want my own van and my own name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd change nothing at work. We'd buy the house, have the wedding we planned, and I'd start Saturdays with my uncle. I'd save a bit for a van in year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. It's like knowing the winter is coming, and you have time to cut wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools to run a bathroom business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire someone to do the paperwork side, my cousin's good with that. I won't touch it myself. If the customer wants a quote, they get my handwriting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't rely on a big company to look after you, because the company will choose the machine. Learn something with your hands that people need in their homes.

say: This is **fair warning**, so nobody can blame anyone if they're not ready.
Fathers should **learn a trade** for their children's sake.
think: I'd still **lose the warehouse job** in the end, I'm sure.
Ten years of Saturdays could give me **my own van** by 2039.
do: Keep the warehouse job **unchanged** in the first year.
Start **Saturdays with his uncle** fitting bathrooms.
Save toward a **van** for year three or four.
feel: Anxious but **quieter**, like having time to cut wood before winter.
S4.quote: Don't rely on a big company to look after you, because the company will choose the machine. Learn something with your hands that people need in their homes.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, he expects the **warehouse job** to go.
He'd keep his **handwritten quotes** and leave AI to his cousin.
The **wedding and house** go ahead as planned here.

steps.text: Keep his warehouse shift unchanged in the first year
Work Saturdays fitting bathrooms with his uncle
Save toward his own work van by year four
Go ahead with the planned wedding and house purchase

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. I'd be married, maybe a father, with a job ending and no trade yet. What would help is a proper paid apprenticeship with a tradesman, not a computer course, so a man can keep earning while he learns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens with the machines, my faith and my family stay. That's what I'd hold on to when the job goes.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with the machines, my faith and my family stay. That's what I'd hold on to when the job goes.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old picker at a **building supplies** warehouse, lifting heavy goods.
He's marrying Samira next summer and wants to be the **main earner** once they have children.
He has never used AI and turns down **optional courses**.
In the fast AGI picture he expects to **lose the job** and is awake doing sums.
His way out is learning **bathroom fitting** from his uncle, though he admits he'd delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with a new marriage, maybe a baby, and no trade yet.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** with a real tradesman, not a computer course.
